title: What are the best investment tracking apps for busy professionals?
summary: Our ranked view of the best investment tracking apps if you work full time, with prices and who each fits. We make Astor, one of the apps listed.
body_markdown:
## The best investment tracking apps, ranked


### 1. Astor: best for being told when something touches what you own


Astor is for people who don’t have time to watch the market. It connects to the brokerage, retirement and crypto accounts you already have at most major US institutions, like Robinhood, Schwab and Coinbase, and follows every position you own along with the earnings dates, filings and headlines that touch them. On Pro and Max, when something crosses a line you care about, it texts you what happened, why it matters to you and what you could do. It stays quiet when nothing matters.


For a quick check,[At a glance](https://www.astor.app/blog/at-a-glance) gives you short daily notes on your portfolio and the market, and every weekday Astor sends a recap after the close. You can[text Astor](https://www.astor.app/blog/talk-to-astor-in-imessage) over iMessage or WhatsApp to ask about what you own, and set[scheduled alerts](https://www.astor.app/blog/scheduled-alerts) , like a check every morning or before a company you own reports.


Astor is free to start with no card, and the free plan includes one custom alert at a time. Pro and Max are in the table above and on our[pricing page](https://www.astor.app/pricing) . There’s no Android app or web app, though people on Android can text Astor on WhatsApp. It’s US only, and it doesn’t do budgeting or track real estate. The AI can be wrong, which is why every alert links to its reasoning and sources and you make the call.


### 2. Empower: the best free dashboard


Empower’s dashboard is free, and it links your investment accounts alongside checking, credit cards, loans and mortgages through Yodlee. Its tools include a retirement planner, a fee analyzer and an Investment Checkup that looks at your portfolio’s risk and past performance and suggests an alternative allocation. It’s a good free place to see your net worth and whether you’re on track for retirement.


Empower’s terms say the dashboard doesn’t give investment advice, and its affiliate, Empower Advisory Group, is an SEC-registered adviser that sells wealth management priced on the assets it manages. Empower says dashboard users may be eligible for a free consultation with one of its advisers.


### 3. Monarch: best for budgeting and investments in one app


Monarch is a budgeting app first, and it tracks investments too, including individual stocks, funds, ETFs, 401(k)s and crypto. It shows your allocation and can pull in your home’s value from Zillow, so your net worth includes it. It costs $14.99 a month or $99.99 a year, and the first week is free.


It’s a good pick if your investing questions come back to your household’s cash flow. Monarch’s terms say it isn’t an investment adviser, and the investment side is a view of your accounts rather than research on them.


### 4. Kubera: best for tracking every kind of asset


Kubera is built for net worth that goes well beyond a brokerage account. It covers 401(k)s, IRAs, RSUs and stock options, crypto wallets and exchanges, precious metals, real estate, vehicles, collectibles and private investments, and it connects through several aggregators including Plaid, MX and Yodlee. Kubera says those connections are read-only and it can’t start transactions.


Essentials costs $250 a year for two portfolios and two users, and there’s a 14-day trial. It runs on the web and as a mobile web app you can install from your browser. If most of your money is in a couple of standard accounts, that price buys more than you need.


### 5. Stock Rover: best for deep stock research and portfolio analytics


Stock Rover is a research platform for people who enjoy the work. Its paid plans add portfolio analytics, rebalancing tools, projected dividend income and real-time email alerts, and it links brokerage accounts through Yodlee. Plans run from $34 a month or $348 a year up to $199 a month for Ultimate Pro, with a 14-day free trial, and the free plan covers basic research only.


In our view it asks more of your time than anything else here, which is the trade-off for its depth. Its terms say it isn’t an investment adviser.


### 6. Morningstar Investor: best for looking inside your funds


Morningstar Investor is the one to use if most of your money is in mutual funds and ETFs. Its X-Ray tool lays out your overall allocation, sector weightings and fees across the funds you own, and Stock Intersection shows where your holdings are concentrated. You can connect accounts and track both total and personal return. It costs $34.95 a month or $249 a year after a seven-day trial, on the web and iPhone.


### 7. Simply Wall St: best for visual stock research


Simply Wall St turns company financials into charts, so a stock is quicker to size up. Its portfolio tracker syncs with more than 2,000 brokers and calculates your returns and dividend income, and it sends daily alerts on earnings, dividends and valuation changes. The free plan covers one portfolio of up to 10 holdings, and Premium and Unlimited are paid. Simply Wall St describes the advice on its site as general advice only.


### 8. Snowball Analytics: best for dividend income


Snowball Analytics is made for income investors. It tracks every dividend automatically and measures performance including fees and dividends, and paid plans add alerts for dividend events. It connects to brokers read-only through Yodlee, SnapTrade and Plaid, or you can import statements. The free plan covers one portfolio of 10 holdings without account linking, and paid plans start at $79.99 a year. Snowball says it isn’t a registered investment adviser.


### 9. Quicken Classic Premier: best for detailed records on a computer


Quicken Classic Premier is desktop software for Windows and Mac, with a mobile companion app. It suits people who want detailed records of everything, from bills to investments, and Quicken lists investment tools like a capital gains estimator, return tracking and Morningstar’s Portfolio X-Ray. Premier is $7.99 a month billed yearly for the first year, and it renews at Quicken’s current rate.
